To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Proprioceptive training is a promising behavioral intervention for improving sensorimoter function; (2) The most effective forms of proprioceptive training are those that utilize passive and active movements and provide visual feedback; (3) Proprioceptive function is most likely improved by the training of both the peripheral and the cortical components of the somatosensory system; and (4) The most effective proprioceptive training is that which is administered for longer durations and with higher frequency.

(1) There is converging, but still preliminary, evidence that proprioceptive rehabilitation can improve sensorimotor function, and that (2) the most promising forms of rehabilitation include both passive and active movement with and without visual guidance.
proprioceptive training, in general, is effective for improving motor function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel, non-pharmacological therapies for improving impaired motor and sensory function.
the role of the somatosensory system, in particular proprioception, in human motor control, learning and recovery.
the role of the proprioceptive system in the development and maintenance of motor function, and the potential to improve sensorimotor function via training of the proprioception system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
proprioceptive training has been proven to be an effective behavioral therapy.
proprioceptive training has the potential to enhance proprioception, and that the effects may be more pronounced in patients with impaired proprioception than in healthy subjects.
proprioceptive training should be incorporated into the rehabilitation of patients suffering from impaired sensorimotor function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effectiveness of proprioceptive interventions is highly variable.
proprioceptive training has a beneficial effect on motor function.
proprioceptive training has a positive impact on somatosensory perception and that this effect can be further enhanced by including active movement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
proprioceptive training has a clear and measurable effect on somatosensory performance and is therefore a viable behavioral intervention.
proprioceptive training has the ability to enhance proprioception and improve sensorimotor function in a wide variety of neurological conditions.
proprioceptive training should not be overlooked as an effective behavioral therapy for improving motor function.
